bridges.statement: Mental properties cannot be identical with or reduced to physical brain properties.
A soul best grounds unified consciousness, indivisible personhood, and identity through change.
Libertarian agency requires a nonphysical personal originator.
Brain dependence is compatible with a soul using the brain as an instrument.
Metaphysical reasoning can establish truths that empirical science alone cannot establish.

routes.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
routes.position: No soul has been shown to exist

bridges.statement: No soul has been reliably demonstrated.
Split-brain and brain-damage observations support dependence of attributed soul functions on brains.
A proposed soul explanation needs a reliable method and evidence of necessity, not mere compatibility.
Physical and emergent accounts remain viable alternatives to a soul.
Any soul that affects material reality should produce detectable manifestations.
Continuing identity can be understood through practical labels applied to changing physical persons.
Agency and rational belief do not require libertarian freedom.

sections.title: Independent Opening Cases
sections.rationale: Covers Hernandez's seven announced independent arguments and Dillahunty's distinct opening standards, neurological evidence, interaction claim, and explanatory objection.

sections.title: Direct Rebuttals
sections.rationale: Covers each speaker's principal rebuttal to the other's opening case, including instrumentality, neuroplasticity, identity labeling, and emergence.

sections.title: Free-Will Cross-Examination
sections.rationale: Covers the first sustained cross-examination exchange over compatibilism, determinism, rationality, and purported demonstrations of freedom.

sections.title: Mind, Identity, and Verification Cross-Examination
sections.rationale: Covers the later cross-examination on verification, mental states, qualia, split-brain identity, and whether soul attributes form a demonstrated entity.

sections.title: Moderated and Audience Questions
sections.rationale: Covers major moderated and audience challenges concerning explanatory gaps, interaction, brain damage, and near-death experiences.

sections.title: Closing Summations
sections.rationale: Covers both final statements of the parties' central burdens and conclusions.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The overall absolute difference is 3 because the complete source contains more separately load-bearing negative replies in the two cross-examination sections. In free-will cross-examination, Hernandez advances two selected substantive moves—the determinism/rationality challenge and the hand-raising demonstration—while Dillahunty supplies four distinct answers: compatibilist agency, truth independent of choice, the programmed-computer counterexample, and causality as the basis of rationality. Combining those answers would erase independently asserted reasoning. In mind, identity, and verification cross-examination, Hernandez supplies three selected moves—the standard for changing his mind, the qualia challenge, and the account of latent capacities—while Dillahunty supplies five distinct moves: the reliable-method standard, the brain-produced-mind answer, the renewed split-brain-individuals claim, the one-package challenge, and the culminating distinction between labeling qualities and demonstrating an entity. These asymmetries arise from the actual sequence and density of distinct answers rather than forced side parity. All seven expressly announced affirmative opening arguments are retained separately; none was omitted.
